title: Anthropic’s ‘Watermark’ Text Adulteration in Claude Is a Perversion of Writing
excerpt: It’s unacceptable for a tool to sacrifice an iota of clarity, coherence, meaning, quality, etc. for the purpose of embedding hidden clues within the text to suggest its provenance. The idea that anything other than *my* needs should factor into the generation of text *for me* is patently offensive.
content_html:
When I wrote this week about Anthropic’s announcement that all Claude models, worldwide, would soon begin “watermarking” everything they generate, including text, to comply with this EU regulation, we were left to speculate how this was going to work, because Anthropic offered not even a vague description of how it would work — despite the fact that the title of the announcement was, absurdly and insultingly, “How Claude Marks AI-Generated Content”.

My initial speculation was that maybe they’d hide invisible non-printing Unicode characters in the text. Just spitballing. Turns out that’s not what they’re going to do. What they’re going to do is apply a form of steganography, where the choice of words (or other token output) at inference time will leave fingerprints that can later, maybe, be detected probabilistically.

I initially guessed “invisible characters” not because I didn’t think of the semantic word-choice technique, but because I was a fool who took Anthropic at its word in their description of what they would do. Their original support document claims:

When a supported Claude model generates text, it weaves an imperceptible watermark directly into the text itself. You won’t see it, and it doesn’t change the meaning, quality, or readability of Claude’s response.

They say “imperceptible” and “doesn’t change the meaning, quality, or readability”. Their words. Not almost imperceptible. Not slightly changes the meaning, quality, or readability. That made sense to me, because that’s absolutely what I want — nay, demand — from any tools I use personally. It’s unacceptable for a tool to sacrifice an iota of clarity, coherence, meaning, quality, etc. for the purpose of embedding hidden clues within the text to suggest its provenance. That’s what I would and will demand. And Anthropic’s (original) support document unambiguously claims that’s what their system will enable. So if that were true, I couldn’t see what was left other than hiding invisible characters within the text.

My error was believing Anthropic that their system wouldn’t adulterate and corrupt the semantics of the text their models generate. That is in fact exactly what they plan to do. I should have my head examined for believing a single word of a document titled “How Claude Marks AI-Generated Content” that doesn’t explain, at all, how Claude marks (or will mark) AI-generated content.

How It’s Actually Going to Work

Yesterday, on an entirely different website than the original “How Claude marks AI-generated content” article (the one that didn’t explain anything at all about how it works), Anthropic published “How Claude’s Text Watermark Works”, which does actually explain in layman-accessible terms how it’s going to work. I will return to Anthropic’s new highly euphemistic and slightly misleading description below.

There’s a bunch of research on this topic, some of which I have also linked to below. But the very best description of the general idea behind the technique is an interactive essay by James Padolsey, “How AI Text Watermarking Works”. It’s a wonderfully cogent read, and the interactive elements splendidly illustrate the main concepts. A+ work. If you have any interest in this at all, I dare say you must read — and play with — Padolsey’s piece.

But here’s my stab at a layman’s high-level summary. If you toss a coin N times and note the results, you can determine with a degree of certainty whether the coin is fair or biased. LLMs are, in their popular incarnations, non-deterministic. Ask the same question of the same model and you often get at least slightly different answers. Maybe the same meaning, but different phrasing. At each decision point for generating the next token, the model makes a choice. With these semantic watermarking techniques, they make different choices for some tokens based on word lists that could be called “green” and “red”. At each decision point, they’re a little more likely to pick a word from the green list than the red list. That doesn’t mean they never choose words from the red list. Just that they’re less likely to than they would if the adulterated marking technique weren’t in place. (Same way that a crooked 51-49 coin will still land “wrong” side up 49 times out of 100 on average.)

Words or word phrases are sorted into the green and red lists deterministically on the fly, at each “next token” generation point. So sometimes a specific word will be on the green list, and other times it will be on the red list. Someone with the secret key can determine which list a word will be on at each token generation point (which is how the watermarking is detected); those without the secret key cannot. This means there will never be a list of words that Claude prefers or eschews.

With coin flipping, the higher N is — the more times you flip — the more confident you can be that the coin is fair or biased. So too with this semantic watermarking. The more words in the text, the more accurate the analysis will be that the text was generated by a specific AI model or not. With too few coin flips, you can’t achieve any confidence at all regarding a coin’s fairness. With too few words (or tokens), there’s no way to achieve any confidence whether a string of text was AI-generated or not.

Given a string of text to examine for signs of a specific watermarking system, if there are more words tagged as green and fewer tagged as red than would otherwise be expected, the text can be flagged — with some degree of confidence — as having been generated, or merely modified, by the AI system that applies the specific secret-key watermarking system. The amount of confidence in the determination will obviously vary, significantly, based on the size of the text string and randomized weights given to words on the green and red lists. But only Anthropic will be able to determine if text was seemingly generated by Claude, and Anthropic will only be able to detect the watermarks that are applied by Claude. Claude can’t detect the hidden watermark signals generated by, say, Gemini, and Gemini can’t detect the hidden watermark signals created by Claude, because each implementation is predicated on secret keys held only by the LLM provider.

Objections to the Technical Premise

One of my fundamental problems with this is that no two synonyms carry the exact same meaning. “He leaped at the chance” and “He jumped at the opportunity” are very similar sentences expressing the same general sentiment, but they are not the same. The exact words we choose when writing matter. I want any LLM I use to choose the very best, most precise words at every single decision point. An obvious constraint that I accept is time and computation. Within the constraint of executing inference quickly, and at a certain cost per token, I want the best words. This constraint matches human writing. I could surely write a better column by taking longer to write it. I write with a sense of how much care I should put into every word and punctuation choice I make. I take more time with certain paragraphs, sentences, or even individual word choices when my gut feeling says I should.

In other words, these are necessary trade-offs. These factors are all in my interest: speed, cost, quality. Ideally I would like perfect writing, at instantaneous generation speed, at zero cost. None of those things are possible. Computation is not free of charge (and cloud-based LLM inference with leading models is actually expensive). Inference is not instantaneous. And great writing, whether natural or artificial, can only approach perfection.

The idea that anything other than my needs should factor into the generation of text for me is patently offensive.

This isn’t just about text one might generate with the intention of passing it off as their own natural work. This isn’t even about LLM proofreading of work written by hand. Anthropic is saying that all new Claude models are going to adulterate every single bit of text longer than 200 tokens (~150 words) they generate, including everything it presents to its users to read. So even in a private conversation between a user and Claude, which will never be read by anyone other than the user, Claude will begin making word choices in the name of marking its output in statistically predictable ways rather than maximizing clarity and precision.

Even today’s so-called frontier models are already decidedly lacking in lucidity. Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, et al. are “better writers” than most humans and produce better prose than the median human. But: no shit. Most people are terrible writers. The “average person” is pretty stupid and half of all people are stupider than that. And there are many smart, interesting people who are miserable writers. So as impressive as LLMs are, the bar is low. The best writing I see come out of these models is worse than anything I would choose to read for pleasure. And now Anthropic is saying they’re going to make it worse, on purpose, for purposes that do not benefit me in any way? Even if only slightly worse?

Get fucked.

Objections to the EU Regulation

Speaking of objections, the relevant EU regulation motivating all of this, “Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content”, is red-tape nanny-state pipe-dream nonsense. Here’s Ben Thompson’s summary from a paywalled Stratechery update this week:

  • The regulation applies to text longer than 200 tokens.
  • The provider must mandate in their terms-of-service that users not remove the watermarking.
  • The solution should be robust in terms of evading “typical processing solutions” like screen shots, scanning and OCR, copy-and-pasting, translations, etc.

Taken literally, compliant LLM terms of service must forbid users from rephrasing the output from models that comply with this regulation, because the word choices are the marks. But it’s not the European Union that is trying to impose their absurd, impractical, witch-hunt-fueling regulation on the entire world. That falls on Anthropic.

Complying with this, particularly with regard to text, is only going to create problems for honest users. Dishonest users attempting to pass off AI-generated text as their own writing (students, employees, whoever) will simply circumvent detection through non-compliant AI paraphrasing tools.

James Padolsey — whose interactive visual explanation of how these schemes work I linked to above — explains this in a post titled “Anthropic’s Weak Watermarks Appease a Weak Law” (which, if it rings a bell, I linked to in a standalone post earlier today):

The same thought that led to this law could have applied to calculators at the time of their inception, had their outputs revealed themselves through artefacts. Thankfully, a sum borne of the brain is treated no differently from one produced by a calculator. Likewise with spellcheckers. To make assistance suspect only once the tool becomes capable enough to compose a whole sentence is not a principled boundary. It is a moral premium placed on difficulty itself.

Anthropic has nevertheless chosen a blanket, model-level implementation that appears broader than the law’s minimum requirement. That may be convenient compliance engineering, but it discards distinctions the law expressly attempted to preserve. The result is a signal broad enough to implicate harmless and assistive use, yet fragile enough to be removed by a motivated person through substantial recomposition. It risks concentrating suspicion on ordinary and assistive users while remaining weakest against deliberate deception.

Padolsey is the creator of Declaude, a delightfully simple web app that allows you to “Paste in AI-flavored text and get the same content back as plain prose”. Declaude’s original purpose is cleaning the saccharine Claude personality stink from text (whether it was created by Claude or any other LLM), but, if Anthropic persists in its stated plan to begin adulterating all text Claude generates, Declaude will also serve as a copy-paste single-extra-step way to eliminates those marks. Declaude is interesting and useful already, but it exemplifies how ill-considered and futile this EU regulation is when it comes to prose.

Google SynthID

Google has a watermarking system in place that they call SynthID, which they apply to AI-generated images, video, audio, and text. I’m concerned in this article only with text. With multimedia, embedded watermarks can be metadata within files, and truly not affect the experiential quality of the work when viewed or listened to. With text, we are talking about the actual words that are chosen. From the “AI-generated text” section of Google DeepMind’s own description of SynthID:

We’ve expanded SynthID to watermarking and identifying text generated by the Gemini app and web experience. Large language models generate text one word (token) at a time. Each word is assigned a probability score, based on how likely it is to be generated next. So for a sentence like “My favorite tropical fruits are mango and…”, the word “bananas” would have a higher probability score than the word “airplanes”. SynthID adjusts these probability scores to generate a watermark. It’s not noticeable to the human eye, and doesn’t affect the quality of the output.

In a group chat, a friend of mine quoted the above, and I responded that if a chatbot wrote “My favorite tropical fruits are mango and airplanes”, I’m pretty sure I’d fucking notice. Another friend then responded with this:

Days later, that still cracks me up.

But Google’s absurd description puts the lie to their own claim that it isn’t noticeable, and it serves to show just how little regard the people behind these generated-text fingerprinting schemes have for the actual craft of writing. Of course bananas has a higher probability score than airplanes, because airplanes aren’t fruit. But what about pineapple? Should the sentence complete to “mango and bananas” or “mango and pineapple”? That’s a good question, and the only acceptable answer for why an LLM should choose bananas instead of pineapple (or coconut, or guava, or papaya...) is that it has determined that it’s the best fit for the intended meaning, tone, and sentiment of the text. Not because bananas is on the watermarking “green” list and pineapple is on the “red” list, even though pineapple might be the better fit. Google’s own supposedly jocular description of how SynthID works in fact captures how the scheme perverts the text it generates.

They’re saying you won’t notice because if it only chooses bananas over pineapple for these fingerprinting purposes, well, they’re both tropical fruits and who cares. But it’s utter nonsense that the difference is “not noticeable to the human eye”. The semantic difference between banana and pineapple is just as noticeable to the human eye as the taste of the two are to the human tongue.

If it did produce “My favorite tropical fruits are mango and airplanes”, it’d be incredibly stupid, but it wouldn’t be offensive because we’d all recognize that something completely off-key happened. What’s offensive is that with a system like SynthId in place, where the fingerprinting decisions are motivated by a secret key, we have no idea whether it completed to “mango and bananas” because bananas was determined to be the best next token, or because bananas is in the “green” bucket of words. It calls every single word choice into question.

Here’s a paper published in Nature where Google’s team behind SynthID published their work, after putting it into production with Gemini (née Bard):

We analysed approximately 20 million watermarked and unwatermarked responses and computed the thumbs-up and thumbs-down rates (both as a fraction of the total number of thumbs-up and thumbs-down feedback received). We found that the thumbs-up rate for the two models differed by 0.01% (with the watermarked model being higher); and the thumbs-down rate differed by 0.02% (with the watermarked model being lower). We found both of these differences to be statistically insignificant, and well within the 95% confidence intervals.

From this experiment, we conclude that over a wide variety of real chatbot interactions, the difference in response quality and utility, as judged by humans, is negligible. Subsequently, non-distortionary SynthID-Text has been productionized and is currently watermarking responses in Gemini and Gemini Advanced. To the best of our knowledge, this evaluation represents the first systematic watermarking investigation of its kind within a large-scale production system.

To this I say:

  • Gemini/Bard’s thumbs-up/thumbs-down buttons are not a good experiment for evaluating the effect on quality. If a chatbot tells me “My favorite tropical fruits are mango and bananas” instead of “mango and pineapple”, I’m not going to give the response a thumbs down because of the fruit it chose. I’d give it a thumbs down if it said “airplanes”, yes, but that’s a strawman. (The paper in Nature even uses “My favourite tropical fruit is ...” as an illustration, but in the paper, the only four next tokens considered are, in order of probability distribution, mango, lychee, papaya, and durian. No airplanes. And, conveniently, in the paper’s example, the “winner” of the watermarking “tournament” just happens to be mango, the one that would have been selected as the best if the watermarking weren’t in place.)

  • A “difference in response quality and utility, as judged by humans” that is “negligible” does not mean imperceptible. What they really mean is that it’s only slightly worse and that everyone is either too stupid to notice or too indifferent to care.

  • It’s widely considered that Gemini is behind ChatGPT and Claude in quality. Perhaps the fact that they’ve put SynthID-text into production is one of many reasons why. I personally agree that Gemini’s prose is inferior. Maybe the use of SynthID has nothing to do with the fact that I, along with the general public consensus, consider Gemini to be a second-rate chatbot — but in that case, maybe it’s the fact that Gemini is a second-rate chatbot that makes the difference “negligible” when Google started mixing in SynthID-motivated tokens in its results. It’s a lot more likely that your restaurant customers won’t notice that you replaced your regular coffee with Folgers Crystals if your regular coffee is second-rate to start with.

Anthropic

Now, finally, back to Anthropic’s new “How Claude’s Text Watermark Works”, published yesterday. I have some comments.

To summarize:

  • We use a method of watermarking that does not have any practical impact on the quality or content of Claude’s outputs;

  • The difference between watermarked and un-watermarked text will not be distinguishable to readers;

Translation: Specific words do not matter and we don’t think anyone reads anything closely.

  • Nothing is added to the text and there are no hidden characters;

This would have been worth clarifying at the outset.

  • Watermarking won’t be specific to Claude. As of August 2, the EU requires AI providers serving its market to mark AI-generated content. Other major model developers have signed the same Code of Practice and will be implementing their own watermarks.

No other AI provider has stated that they will apply such marking, adulterating all generated text, outside the EU.

Take the sentence “The weather today was cold and…”. The next word is very unlikely to be “sugary.” But it is quite likely to be “overcast” or “grey.” Under most circumstances, it doesn’t matter much to the reader which of these latter two words the model ultimately chooses — the meaning of the sentence is largely the same either way. In cases like this, the choice is settled by a random number.

Arguing that grey vs. overcast “doesn’t matter much to the reader” is the crux of my argument that this entire endeavor is a perverse adulteration of what it means to write — or to read. That it’s subtle in some ways makes it more perverse, because it’s sneaky.

In internal testing, we’ve seen no impact of watermarking on the content, level of creativity, or readability of Claude’s text. In the SynthID-Text paper, which introduced the technique we use, Google DeepMind tested this impact by serving a model that used watermarking to a portion of their Gemini traffic and comparing thumbs-up and thumbs-down ratings. They found no statistically significant differences from the unwatermarked model. And in a controlled study, human raters comparing watermarked and unwatermarked answers side-by-side saw no difference in quality.

See above for my argument that this thumbs-up/thumbs-down data is absolutely worthless in evaluating whether the SynthID-style word-bias watermarking makes text worse. By definition it must make text worse, unless the underlying LLM model’s scoring is wrong, because the nature of the watermarking algorithm requires it to sometimes increase the probability of selecting a worse word choice and decrease the probability of selecting the model’s best choice. It’s only a question of how much worse. What Google’s thumb-counting data shows is only that it isn’t so much worse as to make Gemini users click the thumbs-down button.

Watermarking doesn’t change the meaning or experience for the person reading it, but if you wanted to check after the fact whether the text was likely generated by Claude, the watermark allows you to do so.

No, it does not. Because the entire scheme is tied to secret keys held only by the AI provider, it only allows Anthropic, not “you”, to check anything.

When Claude proofreads text written by a person, what it gives back has generally only been lightly edited; because nearly all the words are the person’s, there’s very little (if anything) for the watermark to attach to. Depending on the length of the text and how heavily Claude has edited it, those changes might not be enough to make Claude’s involvement detectable. The more Claude writes, the more decisions it has to make, and the more space there is for a watermark.

Translation: No one can ever again use Claude for proofreading their own prose unless they’re willing to risk that the whole thing might be flagged as having been generated by Claude.

For example, once the model has written “2 + 2 =”, there is a very clear best choice for the next token (if the model is completing the sum, there isn’t an answer that’s equally as good as “4”; if it’s talking about George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four, there isn’t an answer that’s equally as good as “5”). The “nudge” of the watermark wouldn’t be applied here. For the same reason, code — which in very many cases has to be exact — has generally less watermarking than some other forms of text.

Having said that, in areas where there is an arbitrary choice between particular words or terms within the code, the watermark can be used, such as comments within code. But by definition, it will have a negligible effect on the actual code produced.

Translation: We value precision in programming code; we do not in prose.

And it is exceedingly rich to cite George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four, approvingly, in the context of justifying a text adulteration scheme premised on the notion that specific words do not matter. I mean what the actual fuck? Orwell!

Lastly, as to why they’re doing this:

We’re implementing watermarking to comply with the EU AI Act. Anthropic, along with several other major AI model providers and around 190 total signatories, signed the EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content in July 2026. This requires AI system providers to use methods of “marking” AI-generated text. We’re applying watermarking globally at launch because we don’t yet have a durable way to scope it by region.

This, from a company that the Financial Times just reported is weeks away from an IPO with an intended valuation of $2 trillion, which would make it one of the 10 highest-valued companies in the world — as of today, placing it at #7, between TSMC ($2.2T) and Broadcom ($1.9T).

This leaves us to believe that one of the following must be true:

  • It’s perfectly reasonable that a technology company valued on par with Amazon and TSMC is technically incapable of complying with an EU regional law only within the EU itself.1 Not a cause for concern at all.

  • Anthropic is in over their heads, wields shockingly little control over their own tech stack, and their imminent IPO is likely to be remembered only as a new high-water mark in the manic global AI bubble.

Also, what happens if another major global market makes it unlawful for AI to secretly watermark generated text?

OpenAI

From an OpenAI support document titled “Provenance Signals (Content Credentials, SynthID) in OpenAI-Generated Content”:

Consistent with our commitments under the European Commission’s Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated content, our goal is to expand provenance signals to all modalities including text, so customers and developers have clear ways to meet their own transparency obligations as standards and tooling continue to mature.

There’s a lot of wiggle room in this brief statement, and it could just as well mean that OpenAI models will only adulterate text with fingerprint markers when users or developers ask for it. Or that it will only be mandatory for users in the EU. If I were at OpenAI I’d go hard on this and publicly say that ChatGPT will never watermark text it generates unless you ask it to, and that if you want tools that secretly work behind your back without telling you how they work to flag your words in ways you can’t see, go ahead and use Claude.

Further Reading

Three papers on ArXiv:

  • “A Watermark for Large Language Models”, last revised May 2024.
  • “Watermarks in the Sand: Impossibility of Strong Watermarking for Generative Models”, last revised May 2025.
  • “Robust Text Watermarking for Large Language Models via Dual Semantic Embeddings”, last revised June 2026.

I will admit that while I’m profoundly offended by the idea of personally using tools that attempt to leave such watermarks in text they produce or touch, the mathematics behind it are fascinating.

Michael Lopp, at Rands in Repose, “RIP Claude”:

As a human who has had to wrangle with EU regulations in the past, I am abundantly clear what’s involved in the laborious bureaucratic process. I can guess what threats Anthropic is facing. However, this is a tone-deaf, clumsy, and alarming opening salvo in their watermark strategy. [...]

My writing is my work, and Anthropic’s current strategy is aggressively writer-hostile.

Jeff Gamet, “Anthropic’s Claude Watermark Is Akin to an AI Poison Pill”:

To be clear, the watermarking is embedded in pretty much any text Claude touches. Along with text Claude generates, it also applies to text it processes, such as proofreading and summarizing. I expect we’ll see too many inaccurate accusations of using Claude to write documents where the content was human-written, but AI-proofread.

The watermarking sticks with documents through copy-and-paste, too. Imagine copying text from a blog post or email only to have what you wrote tagged as potentially AI-generated. In fact, that could very well happen with this post. I personally write all of my content without AI tools, but I copied the quote at the top of this piece directly from Anthropic’s website. Does that mean what I wrote here will show as AI-generated? If they used their own models to generate or edit what I quoted, then the answer is very likely “yes.”

One of the papers published at ArXiv I cited above claims that such watermarking even persists when an article of text originally generated in English is translated into German.

Secrets are the poison here. When only Anthropic holds the secret keys that both produce the watermarking and perform the probabilistic detection of those marks, we’re all left to wonder. To wonder if what we’re reading is secretly watermarked, what we’re quoting is secretly watermarked, and whether what we ourselves are writing will be unjustly accused of being AI-generated based on secrets we don’t know and can’t see. Poisonous is exactly the right word.

Or should I say toxic? Or airplanes?

Claude can’t detect the hidden watermark signals generated by, say, Gemini, and Gemini can’t detect the hidden watermark signals created by Claude, because each implementation is predicated on secret keys held only by the LLM provider. Objections to the Technical Premise One of my fundamental problems with this is that no two synonyms carry the exact same meaning. “He leaped at the chance” and “He jumped at the opportunity” are very similar sentences expressing the same general sentiment, but they are not the same. The exact words we choose when writing matter. I want any LLM I use to choose the very best, most precise words at every single decision point. An obvious constraint that I accept is time and computation. Within the constraint of executing inference quickly, and at a certain cost per token, I want the best words. This constraint matches human writing. I could surely write a better column by taking longer to write it. I write with a sense of how much care I should put into every word and punctuation choice I make. I take more time with certain paragraphs, sentences, or even individual word choices when my gut feeling says I should. In other words, these are necessary trade-offs. These factors are all in my interest: speed, cost, quality. Ideally I would like perfect writing, at instantaneous generation speed, at zero cost. None of those things are possible. Computation is not free of charge (and cloud-based LLM inference with leading models is actually expensive). Inference is not instantaneous. And great writing, whether natural or artificial, can only approach perfection. The idea that anything other than my needs should factor into the generation of text for me is patently offensive. This isn’t just about text one might generate with the intention of passing it off as their own natural work. This isn’t even about LLM proofreading of work written by hand. Anthropic is saying that all new Claude models are going to adulterate every single bit of text longer than 200 tokens (~150 words) they generate, including everything it presents to its users to read. So even in a private conversation between a user and Claude, which will never be read by anyone other than the user, Claude will begin making word choices in the name of marking its output in statistically predictable ways rather than maximizing clarity and precision. Even today’s so-called frontier models are already decidedly lacking in lucidity. Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, et al. are “better writers” than most humans and produce better prose than the median human. But: no shit. Most people are terrible writers. The “average person” is pretty stupid and half of all people are stupider than that. And there are many smart, interesting people who are miserable writers. So as impressive as LLMs are, the bar is low. The best writing I see come out of these models is worse than anything I would choose to read for pleasure. And now Anthropic is saying they’re going to make it worse, on purpose, for purposes that do not benefit me in any way? Even if only slightly worse? Get fucked. Objections to the EU Regulation Speaking of objections, the relevant EU regulation motivating all of this, “Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content”, is red-tape nanny-state pipe-dream nonsense. Here’s Ben Thompson’s summary from a paywalled Stratechery update this week: The regulation applies to text longer than 200 tokens. The provider must mandate in their terms-of-service that users not remove the watermarking. The solution should be robust in terms of evading “typical processing solutions” like screen shots, scanning and OCR, copy-and-pasting, translations, etc. Taken literally, compliant LLM terms of service must forbid users from rephrasing the output from models that comply with this regulation, because the word choices are the marks. But it’s not the European Union that is trying to impose their absurd, impractical, witch-hunt-fueling regulation on the entire world. That falls on Anthropic. Complying with this, particularly with regard to text, is only going to create problems for honest users. Dishonest users attempting to pass off AI-generated text as their own writing (students, employees, whoever) will simply circumvent detection through non-compliant AI paraphrasing tools. James Padolsey — whose interactive visual explanation of how these schemes work I linked to above — explains this in a post titled “Anthropic’s Weak Watermarks Appease a Weak Law” (which, if it rings a bell, I linked to in a standalone post earlier today): The same thought that led to this law could have applied to calculators at the time of their inception, had their outputs revealed themselves through artefacts. Thankfully, a sum borne of the brain is treated no differently from one produced by a calculator. Likewise with spellcheckers. To make assistance suspect only once the tool becomes capable enough to compose a whole sentence is not a principled boundary. It is a moral premium placed on difficulty itself. Anthropic has nevertheless chosen a blanket, model-level implementation that appears broader than the law’s minimum requirement. That may be convenient compliance engineering, but it discards distinctions the law expressly attempted to preserve. The result is a signal broad enough to implicate harmless and assistive use, yet fragile enough to be removed by a motivated person through substantial recomposition. It risks concentrating suspicion on ordinary and assistive users while remaining weakest against deliberate deception. Padolsey is the creator of Declaude, a delightfully simple web app that allows you to “Paste in AI-flavored text and get the same content back as plain prose”. Declaude’s original purpose is cleaning the saccharine Claude personality stink from text (whether it was created by Claude or any other LLM), but, if Anthropic persists in its stated plan to begin adulterating all text Claude generates, Declaude will also serve as a copy-paste single-extra-step way to eliminates those marks. Declaude is interesting and useful already, but it exemplifies how ill-considered and futile this EU regulation is when it comes to prose. Google SynthID Google has a watermarking system in place that they call SynthID, which they apply to AI-generated images, video, audio, and text. I’m concerned in this article only with text. With multimedia, embedded watermarks can be metadata within files, and truly not affect the experiential quality of the work when viewed or listened to. With text, we are talking about the actual words that are chosen. From the “AI-generated text” section of Google DeepMind’s own description of SynthID: We’ve expanded SynthID to watermarking and identifying text generated by the Gemini app and web experience. Large language models generate text one word (token) at a time. Each word is assigned a probability score, based on how likely it is to be generated next. So for a sentence like “My favorite tropical fruits are mango and…”, the word “bananas” would have a higher probability score than the word “airplanes”. SynthID adjusts these probability scores to generate a watermark. It’s not noticeable to the human eye, and doesn’t affect the quality of the output. In a group chat, a friend of mine quoted the above, and I responded that if a chatbot wrote “My favorite tropical fruits are mango and airplanes”, I’m pretty sure I’d fucking notice. Another friend then responded with this: Days later, that still cracks me up. But Google’s absurd description puts the lie to their own claim that it isn’t noticeable, and it serves to show just how little regard the people behind these generated-text fingerprinting schemes have for the actual craft of writing. Of course bananas has a higher probability score than airplanes, because airplanes aren’t fruit. But what about pineapple? Should the sentence complete to “mango and bananas” or “mango and pineapple”? That’s a good question, and the only acceptable answer for why an LLM should choose bananas instead of pineapple (or coconut, or guava, or papaya...) is that it has determined that it’s the best fit for the intended meaning, tone, and sentiment of the text. Not because bananas is on the watermarking “green” list and pineapple is on the “red” list, even though pineapple might be the better fit. Google’s own supposedly jocular description of how SynthID works in fact captures how the scheme perverts the text it generates. They’re saying you won’t notice because if it only chooses bananas over pineapple for these fingerprinting purposes, well, they’re both tropical fruits and who cares. But it’s utter nonsense that the difference is “not noticeable to the human eye”. The semantic difference between banana and pineapple is just as noticeable to the human eye as the taste of the two are to the human tongue. If it did produce “My favorite tropical fruits are mango and airplanes”, it’d be incredibly stupid, but it wouldn’t be offensive because we’d all recognize that something completely off-key happened. What’s offensive is that with a system like SynthId in place, where the fingerprinting decisions are motivated by a secret key, we have no idea whether it completed to “mango and bananas” because bananas was determined to be the best next token, or because bananas is in the “green” bucket of words. It calls every single word choice into question. Here’s a paper published in Nature where Google’s team behind SynthID published their work, after putting it into production with Gemini (née Bard): We analysed approximately 20 million watermarked and unwatermarked responses and computed the thumbs-up and thumbs-down rates (both as a fraction of the total number of thumbs-up and thumbs-down feedback received). We found that the thumbs-up rate for the two models differed by 0.01% (with the watermarked model being higher); and the thumbs-down rate differed by 0.02% (with the watermarked model being lower). We found both of these differences to be statistically insignificant, and well within the 95% confidence intervals. From this experiment, we conclude that over a wide variety of real chatbot interactions, the difference in response quality and utility, as judged by humans, is negligible. Subsequently, non-distortionary SynthID-Text has been productionized and is currently watermarking responses in Gemini and Gemini Advanced. To the best of our knowledge, this evaluation represents the first systematic watermarking investigation of its kind within a large-scale production system. To this I say: Gemini/Bard’s thumbs-up/thumbs-down buttons are not a good experiment for evaluating the effect on quality. If a chatbot tells me “My favorite tropical fruits are mango and bananas” instead of “mango and pineapple”, I’m not going to give the response a thumbs down because of the fruit it chose. I’d give it a thumbs down if it said “airplanes”, yes, but that’s a strawman. (The paper in Nature even uses “My favourite tropical fruit is ...” as an illustration, but in the paper, the only four next tokens considered are, in order of probability distribution, mango, lychee, papaya, and durian. No airplanes. And, conveniently, in the paper’s example, the “winner” of the watermarking “tournament” just happens to be mango, the one that would have been selected as the best if the watermarking weren’t in place.) A “difference in response quality and utility, as judged by humans” that is “negligible” does not mean imperceptible. What they really mean is that it’s only slightly worse and that everyone is either too stupid to notice or too indifferent to care. It’s widely considered that Gemini is behind ChatGPT and Claude in quality. Perhaps the fact that they’ve put SynthID-text into production is one of many reasons why. I personally agree that Gemini’s prose is inferior. Maybe the use of SynthID has nothing to do with the fact that I, along with the general public consensus, consider Gemini to be a second-rate chatbot — but in that case, maybe it’s the fact that Gemini is a second-rate chatbot that makes the difference “negligible” when Google started mixing in SynthID-motivated tokens in its results. It’s a lot more likely that your restaurant customers won’t notice that you replaced your regular coffee with Folgers Crystals if your regular coffee is second-rate to start with. Anthropic Now, finally, back to Anthropic’s new “How Claude’s Text Watermark Works”, published yesterday. I have some comments. To summarize: We use a method of watermarking that does not have any practical impact on the quality or content of Claude’s outputs; The difference between watermarked and un-watermarked text will not be distinguishable to readers; Translation: Specific words do not matter and we don’t think anyone reads anything closely. Nothing is added to the text and there are no hidden characters; This would have been worth clarifying at the outset. Watermarking won’t be specific to Claude. As of August 2, the EU requires AI providers serving its market to mark AI-generated content. Other major model developers have signed the same Code of Practice and will be implementing their own watermarks. No other AI provider has stated that they will apply such marking, adulterating all generated text, outside the EU. Take the sentence “The weather today was cold and…”. The next word is very unlikely to be “sugary.” But it is quite likely to be “overcast” or “grey.” Under most circumstances, it doesn’t matter much to the reader which of these latter two words the model ultimately chooses — the meaning of the sentence is largely the same either way. In cases like this, the choice is settled by a random number. Arguing that grey vs. overcast “doesn’t matter much to the reader” is the crux of my argument that this entire endeavor is a perverse adulteration of what it means to write — or to read. That it’s subtle in some ways makes it more perverse, because it’s sneaky. In internal testing, we’ve seen no impact of watermarking on the content, level of creativity, or readability of Claude’s text. In the SynthID-Text paper, which introduced the technique we use, Google DeepMind tested this impact by serving a model that used watermarking to a portion of their Gemini traffic and comparing thumbs-up and thumbs-down ratings. They found no statistically significant differences from the unwatermarked model. And in a controlled study, human raters comparing watermarked and unwatermarked answers side-by-side saw no difference in quality. See above for my argument that this thumbs-up/thumbs-down data is absolutely worthless in evaluating whether the SynthID-style word-bias watermarking makes text worse. By definition it must make text worse, unless the underlying LLM model’s scoring is wrong, because the nature of the watermarking algorithm requires it to sometimes increase the probability of selecting a worse word choice and decrease the probability of selecting the model’s best choice. It’s only a question of how much worse. What Google’s thumb-counting data shows is only that it isn’t so much worse as to make Gemini users click the thumbs-down button. Watermarking doesn’t change the meaning or experience for the person reading it, but if you wanted to check after the fact whether the text was likely generated by Claude, the watermark allows you to do so. No, it does not. Because the entire scheme is tied to secret keys held only by the AI provider, it only allows Anthropic, not “you”, to check anything. When Claude proofreads text written by a person, what it gives back has generally only been lightly edited; because nearly all the words are the person’s, there’s very little (if anything) for the watermark to attach to. Depending on the length of the text and how heavily Claude has edited it, those changes might not be enough to make Claude’s involvement detectable. The more Claude writes, the more decisions it has to make, and the more space there is for a watermark. Translation: No one can ever again use Claude for proofreading their own prose unless they’re willing to risk that the whole thing might be flagged as having been generated by Claude. For example, once the model has written “2 + 2 =”, there is a very clear best choice for the next token (if the model is completing the sum, there isn’t an answer that’s equally as good as “4”; if it’s talking about George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four, there isn’t an answer that’s equally as good as “5”). The “nudge” of the watermark wouldn’t be applied here. For the same reason, code — which in very many cases has to be exact — has generally less watermarking than some other forms of text. Having said that, in areas where there is an arbitrary choice between particular words or terms within the code, the watermark can be used, such as comments within code. But by definition, it will have a negligible effect on the actual code produced. Translation: We value precision in programming code; we do not in prose. And it is exceedingly rich to cite George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four, approvingly, in the context of justifying a text adulteration scheme premised on the notion that specific words do not matter. I mean what the actual fuck? Orwell! Lastly, as to why they’re doing this: We’re implementing watermarking to comply with the EU AI Act. Anthropic, along with several other major AI model providers and around 190 total signatories, signed the EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content in July 2026. This requires AI system providers to use methods of “marking” AI-generated text. We’re applying watermarking globally at launch because we don’t yet have a durable way to scope it by region. This, from a company that the Financial Times just reported is weeks away from an IPO with an intended valuation of $2 trillion, which would make it one of the 10 highest-valued companies in the world — as of today, placing it at #7, between TSMC ($2.2T) and Broadcom ($1.9T). This leaves us to believe that one of the following must be true: It’s perfectly reasonable that a technology company valued on par with Amazon and TSMC is technically incapable of complying with an EU regional law only within the EU itself.1 Not a cause for concern at all. Anthropic is in over their heads, wields shockingly little control over their own tech stack, and their imminent IPO is likely to be remembered only as a new high-water mark in the manic global AI bubble. Also, what happens if another major global market makes it unlawful for AI to secretly watermark generated text? OpenAI From an OpenAI support document titled “Provenance Signals (Content Credentials, SynthID) in OpenAI-Generated Content”: Consistent with our commitments under the European Commission’s Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated content, our goal is to expand provenance signals to all modalities including text, so customers and developers have clear ways to meet their own transparency obligations as standards and tooling continue to mature. There’s a lot of wiggle room in this brief statement, and it could just as well mean that OpenAI models will only adulterate text with fingerprint markers when users or developers ask for it. Or that it will only be mandatory for users in the EU. If I were at OpenAI I’d go hard on this and publicly say that ChatGPT will never watermark text it generates unless you ask it to, and that if you want tools that secretly work behind your back without telling you how they work to flag your words in ways you can’t see, go ahead and use Claude. Further Reading Three papers on ArXiv: “A Watermark for Large Language Models”, last revised May 2024. “Watermarks in the Sand: Impossibility of Strong Watermarking for Generative Models”, last revised May 2025. “Robust Text Watermarking for Large Language Models via Dual Semantic Embeddings”, last revised June 2026. I will admit that while I’m profoundly offended by the idea of personally using tools that attempt to leave such watermarks in text they produce or touch, the mathematics behind it are fascinating. Michael Lopp, at Rands in Repose, “RIP Claude”: As a human who has had to wrangle with EU regulations in the past, I am abundantly clear what’s involved in the laborious bureaucratic process. I can guess what threats Anthropic is facing. However, this is a tone-deaf, clumsy, and alarming opening salvo in their watermark strategy. [...] My writing is my work, and Anthropic’s current strategy is aggressively writer-hostile. Jeff Gamet, “Anthropic’s Claude Watermark Is Akin to an AI Poison Pill”: To be clear, the watermarking is embedded in pretty much any text Claude touches. Along with text Claude generates, it also applies to text it processes, such as proofreading and summarizing. I expect we’ll see too many inaccurate accusations of using Claude to write documents where the content was human-written, but AI-proofread. The watermarking sticks with documents through copy-and-paste, too. Imagine copying text from a blog post or email only to have what you wrote tagged as potentially AI-generated. In fact, that could very well happen with this post. I personally write all of my content without AI tools, but I copied the quote at the top of this piece directly from Anthropic’s website. Does that mean what I wrote here will show as AI-generated? If they used their own models to generate or edit what I quoted, then the answer is very likely “yes.” One of the papers published at ArXiv I cited above claims that such watermarking even persists when an article of text originally generated in English is translated into German. Secrets are the poison here. When only Anthropic holds the secret keys that both produce the watermarking and perform the probabilistic detection of those marks, we’re all left to wonder. To wonder if what we’re reading is secretly watermarked, what we’re quoting is secretly watermarked, and whether what we ourselves are writing will be unjustly accused of being AI-generated based on secrets we don’t know and can’t see. Poisonous is exactly the right word. Or should I say toxic? Or airplanes? This is the side that noted savant Jim Cramer is on. ↩︎

blocks.html_en: But here’s my stab at a layman’s high-level summary. If you toss a coin N times and note the results, you can determine with a degree of certainty whether the coin is fair or biased. LLMs are, in their popular incarnations, non-deterministic. Ask the same question of the same model and you often get at least slightly different answers. Maybe the same meaning, but different phrasing. At each decision point for generating the next token, the model makes a choice. With these semantic watermarking techniques, they make different choices for some tokens based on word lists that could be called “green” and “red”. At each decision point, they’re a little more likely to pick a word from the green list than the red list. That doesn’t mean they never choose words from the red list. Just that they’re less likely to than they would if the adulterated marking technique weren’t in place. (Same way that a crooked 51-49 coin will still land “wrong” side up 49 times out of 100 on average.)

blocks.html_en: Words or word phrases are sorted into the green and red lists deterministically on the fly, at each “next token” generation point. So sometimes a specific word will be on the green list, and other times it will be on the red list. Someone with the secret key can determine which list a word will be on at each token generation point (which is how the watermarking is detected); those without the secret key cannot. This means there will never be a list of words that Claude prefers or eschews.

blocks.html_en: With coin flipping, the higher N is — the more times you flip — the more confident you can be that the coin is fair or biased. So too with this semantic watermarking. The more words in the text, the more accurate the analysis will be that the text was generated by a specific AI model or not. With too few coin flips, you can’t achieve any confidence at all regarding a coin’s fairness. With too few words (or tokens), there’s no way to achieve any confidence whether a string of text was AI-generated or not.

sentences.zh: 抛硬币时，N 越高（抛硬币的次数越多），您就越有信心硬币是公平的还是有偏见的。

sentences.zh: 文本中的单词越多，分析该文本是否由特定人工智能模型生成的就越准确。

sentences.zh: 如果抛硬币的次数太少，你就无法对硬币的公平性产生任何信心。

sentences.en: With too few words (or tokens), there’s no way to achieve any confidence whether a string of text was AI-generated or not.
sentences.zh: 如果单词（或标记）太少，就无法确定一串文本是否是人工智能生成的。

blocks.html_en: Given a string of text to examine for signs of a specific watermarking system, if there are more words tagged as green and fewer tagged as red than would otherwise be expected, the text can be flagged — with some degree of confidence — as having been generated, or merely modified, by the AI system that applies the specific secret-key watermarking system. The amount of confidence in the determination will obviously vary, significantly, based on the size of the text string and randomized weights given to words on the green and red lists. But only Anthropic will be able to determine if text was seemingly generated by Claude, and Anthropic will only be able to detect the watermarks that are applied by Claude. Claude can’t detect the hidden watermark signals generated by, say, Gemini, and Gemini can’t detect the hidden watermark signals created by Claude, because each implementation is predicated on secret keys held only by the LLM provider.

blocks.html_en: One of my fundamental problems with this is that no two synonyms carry the exact same meaning. “He leaped at the chance” and “He jumped at the opportunity” are very similar sentences expressing the same general sentiment, but they are not the same. The exact words we choose when writing matter. I want any LLM I use to choose the very best, most precise words at every single decision point. An obvious constraint that I accept is time and computation. Within the constraint of executing inference quickly, and at a certain cost per token, I want the best words. This constraint matches human writing. I could surely write a better column by taking longer to write it. I write with a sense of how much care I should put into every word and punctuation choice I make. I take more time with certain paragraphs, sentences, or even individual word choices when my gut feeling says I should.

blocks.html_en: This isn’t just about text one might generate with the intention of passing it off as their own natural work. This isn’t even about LLM proofreading of work written by hand. Anthropic is saying that all new Claude models are going to adulterate every single bit of text longer than 200 tokens (~150 words) they generate, including everything it presents to its users to read. So even in a private conversation between a user and Claude, which will never be read by anyone other than the user, Claude will begin making word choices in the name of marking its output in statistically predictable ways rather than maximizing clarity and precision.

blocks.html_en: Even today’s so-called frontier models are already decidedly lacking in lucidity. blocks.html_en:
The same thought that led to this law could have applied to calculators at the time of their inception, had their outputs revealed themselves through artefacts. Thankfully, a sum borne of the brain is treated no differently from one produced by a calculator. Likewise with spellcheckers. To make assistance suspect only once the tool becomes capable enough to compose a whole sentence is not a principled boundary. It is a moral premium placed on difficulty itself.

Anthropic has nevertheless chosen a blanket, model-level implementation that appears broader than the law’s minimum requirement. That may be convenient compliance engineering, but it discards distinctions the law expressly attempted to preserve. The result is a signal broad enough to implicate harmless and assistive use, yet fragile enough to be removed by a motivated person through substantial recomposition. It risks concentrating suspicion on ordinary and assistive users while remaining weakest against deliberate deception.

blocks.html_en: We’ve expanded SynthID to watermarking and identifying text generated by the Gemini app and web experience. Large language models generate text one word (token) at a time. blocks.html_en: But Google’s absurd description puts the lie to their own claim that it isn’t noticeable, and it serves to show just how little regard the people behind these generated-text fingerprinting schemes have for the actual craft of writing. Of course bananas has a higher probability score than airplanes, because airplanes aren’t fruit. But what about pineapple? Should the sentence complete to “mango and bananas” or “mango and pineapple”? That’s a good question, and the only acceptable answer for why an LLM should choose bananas instead of pineapple (or coconut, or guava, or papaya...) is that it has determined that it’s the best fit for the intended meaning, tone, and sentiment of the text. Google’s own supposedly jocular description of how SynthID works in fact captures how the scheme perverts the text it generates.

sentences.zh: 以下是《自然》杂志上发表的一篇论文，其中 SynthID 背后的 Google 团队在与 Gemini（née Bard）一起投入生产后发表了他们的研究成果：

blocks.html_en:
We analysed approximately 20 million watermarked and unwatermarked responses and computed the thumbs-up and thumbs-down rates (both as a fraction of the total number of thumbs-up and thumbs-down feedback received). We found that the thumbs-up rate for the two models differed by 0.01% (with the watermarked model being higher); and the thumbs-down rate differed by 0.02% (with the watermarked model being lower). We found both of these differences to be statistically insignificant, and well within the 95% confidence intervals.

From this experiment, we conclude that over a wide variety of real chatbot interactions, the difference in response quality and utility, as judged by humans, is negligible. Subsequently, non-distortionary SynthID-Text has been productionized and is currently watermarking responses in Gemini and Gemini Advanced. To the best of our knowledge, this evaluation represents the first systematic watermarking investigation of its kind within a large-scale production system.

blocks.html_en: See above for my argument that this thumbs-up/thumbs-down data is absolutely worthless in evaluating whether the SynthID-style word-bias watermarking makes text worse. By definition it must make text worse, unless the underlying LLM model’s scoring is wrong, because the nature of the watermarking algorithm requires it to sometimes increase the probability of selecting a worse word choice and decrease the probability of selecting the model’s best choice. content_html_zh:
当我本周写到 Anthropic 宣布全球所有 Claude 模型将很快开始为它们生成的所有内容（包括文本）添加“水印”，以遵守这项欧盟法规时，我们只能猜测这将如何运作，因为 Anthropic 甚至没有提供其如何运作的模糊描述 - 尽管该公告的标题荒谬且侮辱性地是“Claude 如何标记人工智能生成的内容”。

我最初的猜测是，也许他们会在文本中隐藏不可见的非打印 Unicode 字符。 只是吐口水而已。 事实证明这不是他们要做的。 他们要做的是应用一种隐写术，在推理时选择的单词（或其他令牌输出）将留下指纹，这些指纹可能稍后可以被概率性地检测到。

我最初猜测“隐形字符”并不是因为我没有想到语义选词技术，而是因为我是个傻瓜，在他们的描述中相信了 Anthropic 所说的他们会做什么。 他们的原始支持文件声称：

当受支持的 Claude 模型生成文本时，它会将难以察觉的水印直接编织到文本本身中。 你不会看到它，它也不会改变克劳德回应的含义、质量或可读性。

他们说“难以察觉”和“不会改变含义、质量或可读性”。 他们的话。 并非几乎难以察觉。 含义、质量或可读性不会发生轻微改变。 这对我来说很有意义，因为这绝对是我想要的——不，是要求——从我个人使用的任何工具中得到的。 对于一个工具来说，为了在文本中嵌入隐藏的线索来暗示其出处，而牺牲一点清晰度、连贯性、意义、质量等，这是不可接受的。 这就是我愿意并且将会要求的。 Anthropic 的（原始）支持文件明确声称他们的系统将实现这一点。 因此，如果这是真的，除了隐藏文本中不可见的字符之外，我看不到还剩下什么。

我的错误是相信 Anthropic 他们的系统不会掺假和破坏他们的模型生成的文本的语义。 事实上，这正是他们计划做的。 我应该检查一下我的大脑是否相信标题为“克劳德如何标记​​人工智能生成的内容”的文档中的一个单词，该文档根本没有解释克劳德如何标记​​（或将标记）人工智能生成的内容。

它实际上是如何运作的

昨天，在一个与最初的“克劳德如何标记​​人工智能生成的内容”文章（完全没有解释其工作原理的文章）完全不同的网站上，Anthropic 发布了“克劳德的文本水印如何工作”，它实际上用外行人可以理解的术语解释了它是如何工作的。 下面我将回到 Anthropic 的新的高度委婉且略带误导性的描述。

关于这个主题有很多研究，我也在下面链接了其中一些。 但对该技术背后的总体思想的最好描述是 James Padolsey 的一篇互动文章“AI 文本水印如何工作”。 这是一本非常令人信服的读物，互动元素出色地阐释了主要概念。 A+ 工作。 如果你对此有任何兴趣，我敢说你必须阅读并尝试一下帕多尔西的作品。

但这是我对外行人的高层次总结。 如果你抛硬币 N 次并记下结果，你就可以在一定程度上确定这枚硬币是公平的还是有偏见的。 就其流行的形式而言，法学硕士是不确定性的。 问同一型号的同一问题，您经常会得到至少略有不同的答案。 也许意思相同，但措辞不同。 在生成下一个令牌的每个决策点，模型都会做出选择。 通过这些语义水印技术，他们根据可以称为“绿色”和“红色”的单词列表对某些标记做出不同的选择。 在每个决策点，他们从绿色列表中选择单词的可能性比从红色列表中选择单词的可能性要大一些。 这并不意味着他们从不从红色名单中选择单词。 只是如果掺假标记技术没有到位的话，他们这样做的可能性就更小了。 （同样的道理，一枚弯曲的 51-49 硬币在 100 次中平均仍有 49 次“错误”一面朝上落地。）

在每个“下一个标记”生成点，单词或单词短语被确定性地动态分类到绿色和红色列表中。 因此，有时某个特定单词会出现在绿名单上，有时则会出现在红名单上。 拥有秘密密钥的人可以确定单词在每个令牌生成点将出现在哪个列表中（这就是检测水印的方式）；没有密钥的人不能。 这意味着永远不会有克劳德喜欢或回避的单词列表。

抛硬币时，N 越高（抛硬币的次数越多），您就越有信心硬币是公平的还是有偏见的。 这种语义水印也是如此。 文本中的单词越多，分析该文本是否由特定人工智能模型生成的就越准确。 如果抛硬币的次数太少，你就无法对硬币的公平性产生任何信心。 如果单词（或标记）太少，就无法确定一串文本是否是人工智能生成的。

给定一串文本来检查特定水印系统的迹象，如果标记为绿色的单词比预期的多，标记为红色的单词少于预期，则可以以一定程度的置信度将该文本标记为已由应用特定密钥水印系统的人工智能系统生成或仅修改。 根据文本字符串的大小以及赋予绿色和红色列表上的单词的随机权重，确定的置信度显然会显着变化。 但只有 Anthropic 能够确定文本是否看似由 Claude 生成，并且 Anthropic 只能检测 Claude 应用的水印。 例如，Claude 无法检测到由 Gemini 生成的隐藏水印信号，而 Gemini 也无法检测到 Claude 创建的隐藏水印信号，因为每个实现都基于仅由 LLM 提供者持有的密钥。

对技术前提的反对

我对此的基本问题之一是没有两个同义词具有完全相同的含义。 “他抓住了机会”和“他抓住了机会”是非常相似的句子，表达了相同的总体情感，但它们并不相同。 我们在写作时选择的确切词语很重要。 我希望我使用的任何法学硕士都能在每个决策点选择最好、最精确的词语。 我接受的一个明显的限制是时间和计算。 在快速执行推理的约束下，并且每个标记有一定的成本，我想要最好的单词。 这个限制符合人类的书写。 如果我花更长的时间来写，我肯定可以写出更好的专栏。 我写作时会意识到我应该对我所做的每一个单词和标点符号的选择给予多少关注。 当我的直觉告诉我应该花更多时间处理某些段落、句子，甚至单个单词的选择时，我会花更多的时间。

换句话说，这些都是必要的权衡。 这些因素都符合我的利益：速度、成本、质量。 理想情况下，我希望以瞬时生成速度、零成本实现完美的写作。 这些都是不可能的。 计算并不是免费的（基于云的 LLM 推理与领先模型实际上很昂贵）。 推理不是瞬时的。 伟大的写作，无论是自然的还是人工的，都只能接近完美。

认为除了我的需求之外的任何事情都应该被纳入为我生成文本的想法显然是令人反感的。

这不仅仅是人们为了将其冒充为自己的自然作品而生成的文本。 这甚至与法学硕士对手写作品的校对无关。 Anthropic 表示，所有新的 Claude 模型都将掺假它们生成的超过 200 个标记（约 150 个单词）的每一个文本位，包括它呈现给用户阅读的所有内容。 因此，即使在用户和克劳德之间的私人对话中（除了用户之外的任何人都不会阅读该对话），克劳德也会开始以统计上可预测的方式标记其输出的名义做出单词选择，而不是最大化清晰度和精确度。

即使是今天所谓的前沿模型也明显缺乏清晰度。 克劳德、ChatGPT、Grok 等人。是比大多数人“更好的作家”，并且比普通人写出更好的散文。 但是：没什么。 大多数人都是糟糕的作家。 “普通人”非常愚蠢，一半的人比这更愚蠢。 有很多聪明、有趣的人却是悲惨的作家。 尽管法学硕士令人印象深刻，但门槛却很低。 我从这些模型中看到的最好的作品比我为了消遣而选择阅读的任何东西都要糟糕。 现在，Anthropic 说他们会故意让事情变得更糟，以达到对我没有任何好处的目的？ 即使只是稍微差一点？

滚蛋吧。

对欧盟法规的反对

说到反对意见，推动这一切的相关欧盟法规，即《人工智能生成内容透明度实践准则》，是官僚主义保姆国家的白日梦。 以下是 Ben Thompson 在本周付费专区 Stratechery 更新中的总结：

该规定适用于长度超过 200 个标记的文本。 提供商必须在其服务条款中强制用户不得删除水印。 该解决方案在规避“典型处理解决方案”（如屏幕截图、扫描和 OCR、复制粘贴、翻译等）方面应该是稳健的。

从字面上看，合规的 LLM 服务条款必须禁止用户重新表述符合此规定的模型的输出，因为单词选择就是标记。 但试图将其荒谬、不切实际、煽动政治迫害的监管强加给全世界的并不是欧盟。 这落在了人类身上。

遵守这一点，特别是在文本方面，只会给诚实的用户带来问题。 试图将人工智能生成的文本冒充为自己写作的不诚实用户（学生、员工等）只会通过不合规的人工智能释义工具来规避检测。

James Padolsey（我在上面链接到了他对这些方案如何运作的交互式视觉解释）在题为“Anthropic 的弱水印安抚弱法律”的帖子中解释了这一点（如果它响起，我在今天早些时候的独立帖子中链接到）：

如果计算器的输出通过人工制品展现出来的话，导致该定律的相同想法也可以应用于计算器诞生时的情况。 值得庆幸的是，大脑产生的总和与计算器产生的总和没有什么不同。 拼写检查器也是如此。 仅当该工具有足够能力组成一个完整的句子时才对协助产生怀疑，这并不是一个原则性的界限。 这是对困难本身的道德溢价。 尽管如此，Anthropic 选择了一种全面的、模型级的实施方式，其范围似乎比法律的最低要求更广泛。 这可能是方便的合规工程，但它放弃了法律明确试图保留的区别。 结果是一个信号足够广泛，足以暗示无害和辅助使用，但又足够脆弱，可以被有动力的人通过实质性重组去除。 它有可能将怀疑集中在普通用户和辅助用户身上，同时在防范故意欺骗方面表现最弱。

Padolsey 是 Declaude 的创建者，Declaude 是一款非常简单的网络应用程序，可让您“粘贴人工智能风格的文本，并获得与普通散文相同的内容”。 Declaude 的最初目的是清除文本中甜蜜的 Claude 人格臭味（无论它是由 Claude 还是任何其他法学硕士创建的），但是，如果 Anthropic 坚持其既定计划开始掺假 Claude 生成的所有文本，Declaude 也将作为一种复制粘贴单步额外方法来消除这些标记。 Declaude 已经很有趣且有用，但它说明了欧盟的这项法规在散文方面是多么考虑不周和徒劳。

谷歌合成ID

谷歌有一个名为 SynthID 的水印系统，可应用于人工智能生成的图像、视频、音频和文本。 我在这篇文章中只关心文本。 对于多媒体，嵌入的水印可以是文件内的元数据，并且真正不会影响观看或收听时的作品体验质量。 对于文本，我们谈论的是实际选择的单词。 来自 Google DeepMind 自己对 SynthID 的描述的“AI 生成的文本”部分：

我们已将 SynthID 扩展到水印和识别由 Gemini 应用程序和网络体验生成的文本。 大型语言模型一次生成一个单词（标记）文本。 每个单词都会根据接下来生成的可能性分配一个概率分数。 因此，对于像“我最喜欢的热带水果是芒果和......”这样的句子，“香蕉”一词的概率得分高于“飞机”一词。 SynthID 调整这些概率分数以生成水印。 人眼无法察觉，并且不会影响输出的质量。

在一次群聊中，我的一个朋友引用了上述内容，我回答说，如果一个聊天机器人写下“我最喜欢的热带水果是芒果和飞机”，我很确定我他妈会注意到。 随后另一位朋友也回应道：

几天后，这仍然让我感到震惊。

但谷歌荒谬的描述证明了他们自己的说法，即它不引人注目，而且它表明了这些生成文本指纹识别方案背后的人们对实际的书写技巧是多么的不重视。 当然，香蕉的概率得分比飞机更高，因为飞机不是水果。 但是菠萝呢？ 句子应该完整为“芒果和香蕉”还是“芒果和菠萝”？ 这是一个很好的问题，也是为什么法学硕士应该选择香蕉而不是菠萝（或椰子，或番石榴，或木瓜......）的唯一可接受的答案。 是它已经确定它最适合文本的预期含义、语气和情感。 并不是因为香蕉位于水印“绿色”列表中而菠萝位于“红色”列表中，尽管菠萝可能更适合。 谷歌自己对 SynthID 工作原理的看似诙谐的描述实际上捕捉到了该方案如何歪曲其生成的文本。

他们说你不会注意到，因为如果它只选择香蕉而不是菠萝来进行指纹识别，那么，它们都是热带水果，谁在乎呢。 但如果说这种差异“肉眼无法察觉”，那就完全是无稽之谈。 香蕉和菠萝之间的语义差异对于人眼来说就像两者的味道对于人的舌头来说一样明显。

如果它确实产生了“我最喜欢的热带水果是芒果和飞机”，那将是非常愚蠢的，但它不会令人反感，因为我们都会意识到发生了完全跑调的事情。 令人反感的是，使用像 SynthId 这样的系统，指纹识别决策是由密钥驱动的，我们不知道它是否完成为“芒果和香蕉”，因为香蕉被确定为最好的下一个标记，或者因为香蕉位于“绿色”单词桶中。 它使每一个单词的选择都受到质疑。

以下是《自然》杂志上发表的一篇论文，其中 SynthID 背后的 Google 团队在与 Gemini（née Bard）一起投入生产后发表了他们的研究成果：

我们分析了大约 2000 万个带水印和未带水印的回复，并计算了赞成和反对率（均占收到的赞成和反对反馈总数的一小部分）。 我们发现两个模型的点赞率相差0.01%（带水印的模型更高）；不赞成率相差 0.02%（带水印的模型较低）。 我们发现这两个差异在统计上都不显着，并且完全在 95% 置信区间内。 从这个实验中，我们得出的结论是，在各种真实的聊天机器人交互中，根据人类的判断，响应质量和效用的差异可以忽略不计。 随后，非失真 SynthID-Text 已投入生产，目前正在 Gemini 和 Gemini Advanced 中对响应加水印。 据我们所知，这次评估代表了大规模生产系统中同类的首次系统水印调查。

对此我想说：

  • Gemini/Bard 的赞成/反对按钮并不是评估质量影响的良好实验。 如果聊天机器人告诉我“我最喜欢的热带水果是芒果和香蕉”而不是“芒果和菠萝”，我不会因为它选择的水果而对这个回应表示反对。 如果它说“飞机”，我会竖起大拇指，是的，但那是一个稻草人。 （《自然》杂志上的论文甚至使用了“我最喜欢的热带水果是……” 作为说明，但在论文中，按照概率分布的顺序，接下来考虑的唯一四个标记是芒果、荔枝、木瓜和榴莲。 没有飞机。 而且，方便的是，在论文的例子中，水印“锦标赛”的“获胜者”恰好是芒果，如果水印没有到位，芒果就会被选为最好的芒果。）
  • “人类判断的响应质量和效用的差异”“可忽略不计”并不意味着不可察觉。 他们真正的意思是，情况只是稍微糟糕一点，每个人要么太愚蠢而没有注意到，要么太冷漠而没有在意。
  • 人们普遍认为 Gemini 在质量上落后于 ChatGPT 和 Claude。 也许他们将 SynthID-text 投入生产是众多原因之一。 我个人认为双子座的散文较差。 也许 SynthID 的使用与我以及公众的共识认为 Gemini 是二流聊天机器人这一事实无关——但在这种情况下，也许是 Gemini 是二流聊天机器人这一事实使得当 Google 开始在其结果中混合 SynthID 驱动的代币时，差异“可以忽略不计”。 如果您的普通咖啡一开始就是二流的，那么您的餐厅顾客很可能不会注意到您用 Fogers Crystals 代替了普通咖啡。

人择

现在，最后，回到 Anthropic 昨天发布的新书《克劳德的文本水印如何工作》。 我有一些意见。

总结一下：我们使用的水印方法不会对 Claude 输出的质量或内容产生任何实际影响；读者将无法区分带水印和未带水印的文本之间的差异；

翻译：具体的单词并不重要，我们认为没有人会仔细阅读任何内容。

文本中没有添加任何内容，也没有隐藏字符；

这在一开始就值得澄清。

水印并不是克劳德特有的。 自 8 月 2 日起，欧盟要求为其市场提供服务的人工智能提供商对人工智能生成的内容进行标记。 其他主要模型开发商也签署了相同的行为准则，并将实施自己的水印。

没有其他人工智能提供商表示他们将在欧盟以外应用此类标记，掺假所有生成的文本。

就拿这句话来说：“今天的天气很冷……”。 下一个词不太可能是“糖”。 但它很可能是“阴”或“灰色”。 在大多数情况下，模型最终选择后两个单词中的哪一个对于读者来说并不重要——无论哪种方式，句子的含义基本上是相同的。 在这种情况下，选择是由随机数决定的。

认为灰色与阴天“对读者来说并不重要”是我的论点的关键，我的整个努力是对写作或阅读含义的不正当掺假。 它在某些方面的微妙使它变得更加反常，因为它是鬼鬼祟祟的。

在内部测试中，我们发现水印对克劳德文本的内容、创造力水平或可读性没有影响。 在 SynthID-Text 论文中，介绍了我们使用的技术，Google DeepMind 通过提供一个模型来测试这种影响，该模型对部分 Gemini 流量使用水印，并比较赞成和反对的评级。 他们发现与无水印模型没有统计上的显着差异。 在一项对照研究中，人类评分者并排比较带水印和未带水印的答案时发现质量没有差异。

请参阅上面我的论点，即在评估 SynthID 样式的单词偏差水印是否使文本变得更糟时，这些赞成/反对数据绝对毫无价值。 根据定义，它必须使文本变得更糟，除非底层 LLM 模型的评分是错误的，因为水印算法的性质要求它有时会增加选择更差单词的概率，并降低选择模型最佳选择的概率。 这只是一个更糟糕的问题。 谷歌的拇指计数数据仅表明，它并没有比让双子座用户点击拇指向下按钮更糟糕。

水印不会改变阅读者的含义或体验，但如果您想事后检查文本是否可能是由克劳德生成的，水印可以让您这样做。

不，事实并非如此。 因为整个方案与仅由人工智能提供商持有的密钥绑定，所以它只允许人类（而不是“你”）检查任何内容。

当克劳德校对一个人写的文本时，它返回的内容通常只是经过轻微编辑；因为几乎所有的文字都是该人的，所以几乎没有（如果有的话）可以附加水印。 根据文本的长度以及克劳德对其进行编辑的程度，这些更改可能不足以使克劳德的参与被察觉。 克劳德写得越多，需要做出的决定就越多，水印的空间就越大。

翻译：没有人可以再次使用克劳德来校对自己的散文，除非他们愿意冒整个事情可能被标记为克劳德生成的风险。

例如，一旦模型写出“2 + 2 =”，下一个标记就有一个非常明确的最佳选择（如果模型正在完成求和，则没有一个与“4”一样好的答案；如果正在谈论乔治·奥威尔的《十九八十四》，则没有一个与“5”一样好的答案）。 水印的“轻推”不会在这里应用。 出于同样的原因，代码（在很多情况下必须准确）通常比其他一些形式的文本具有更少的水印。 话虽如此，在代码中特定单词或术语之间存在任意选择的区域中，可以使用水印，例如代码中的注释。 但根据定义，它对实际生成的代码的影响可以忽略不计。

翻译：我们重视编程代码的精度；我们不在散文中。

在证明文本掺假计划的合理性的背景下，引用乔治·奥威尔的《十九八十四》是极其丰富的，而这个计划的前提是特定的单词并不重要。 我的意思是，到底是什么？ 奥威尔！

开放人工智能

来自标题为“OpenAI 生成的内容中的来源信号（内容凭证、SynthID）”的 OpenAI 支持文档：

根据我们对欧盟委员会关于人工智能生成内容透明度的行为准则的承诺，我们的目标是将出处信号扩展到包括文本在内的所有模式，以便随着标准和工具的不断成熟，客户和开发人员有明确的方法来履行自己的透明度义务。

这个简短的声明中有很大的回旋余地，这也可能意味着 OpenAI 模型只会在用户或开发人员要求时才会在文本中掺入指纹标记。 或者仅对欧盟用户强制。 如果我在 OpenAI，我会坚决反对这一点，并公开表示，除非您要求，否则 ChatGPT 永远不会为它生成的文本添加水印，并且如果您想要在背后秘密工作而不告诉您它们如何以您看不到的方式标记您的单词的工具，请继续使用 Claude。

进一步阅读

ArXiv 上的三篇论文：

  • “大型语言模型的水印”，最后修订于 2024 年 5 月。
  • “沙子里的水印：生成模型强水印的不可能”，最后修订于 2025 年 5 月。
  • “通过双重语义嵌入为大型语言模型提供鲁棒的文本水印”，最后修订于 2026 年 6 月。

我承认，虽然我对个人使用试图在其生成或触摸的文本中留下此类水印的工具的想法感到深深的冒犯，但其背后的数学是令人着迷的。

迈克尔·洛普 (Michael Lopp)，《Rands in Repose》，《RIP Claude》：

作为一个过去不得不与欧盟法规争论的人，我非常清楚繁琐的官僚程序涉及什么。 我能猜到 Anthropic 面临着什么威胁。 然而，这在他们的水印策略中是一个充耳不闻、笨拙且令人震惊的开场齐射。 [...] 我的写作就是我的工作，而 Anthropic 目前的策略是对作家充满敌意。

Jeff Gamet，“Anthropic 的克劳德水印类似于人工智能毒丸”：

需要明确的是，水印几乎嵌入在克劳德接触的所有文本中。 除了 Claude 生成的文本之外，它还适用于其处理的文本，例如校对和摘要。 我预计我们会看到太多不准确的指控，即使用克劳德编写内容由人工编写但由人工智能校对的文档。 通过复制和粘贴，水印也会粘在文档上。 想象一下，从博客文章或电子邮件中复制文本，只是将您所写的内容标记为可能由人工智能生成。 事实上，这篇文章很可能会发生这种情况。 我个人在没有使用人工智能工具的情况下编写了所有内容，但我直接从 Anthropic 的网站复制了本文顶部的引用。 这是否意味着我在这里写的内容将显示为人工智能生成的？ 如果他们使用自己的模型来生成或编辑我引用的内容，那么答案很可能是“是”。

我在上面引用的 ArXiv 上发表的一篇论文声称，当一篇最初用英语生成的文本被翻译成德语时，这种水印甚至仍然存在。

秘密是这里的毒药。 当只有 Anthropic 拥有既能产生水印又能对这些标记进行概率检测的密钥时，我们都想知道。 想知道我们正在阅读的内容是否被秘密加了水印，我们引用的内容是否被秘密加了水印，以及我们自己所写的内容是否会被不公正地指责为人工智能根据我们不知道也看不到的秘密生成的内容。 有毒这个词用得恰到好处。
